\begin{abstract}
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models consume hundreds of vision tokens per frame, creating a computational bottleneck for real-time robotic control. Token pruning offers a training-free remedy, yet whether a pruning strategy transfers across architectures is untested: removing 5\% of tokens collapses one VLA to near-zero success while another retains full performance.
We conduct a systematic study of token compressibility across six VLA architectures (450M--7B parameters), three vision-connector families, and four LIBERO manipulation suites.
Two axes govern the pruning response and interact to produce a \emph{double dissociation}.
Along the \textbf{coupling axis}, token-independent connectors (linear projections, MLPs) degrade gracefully, while token-entangling connectors (pixel-shuffle, learned encoders) exhibit threshold cliffs or complete collapse.
Along the \textbf{complexity axis}, multi-step tasks amplify entangling-connector losses by up to $20{\times}$ relative to single-step tasks, whereas independent connectors show ${\leq}$11\,pp amplification under the same conditions.
The two axes cross in scoring-method effectiveness: attention-based selection recovers $+$31\,pp on an entangling connector but degrades performance ($-$2 to $-$30\,pp) on an independent one; norm-based selection shows the converse.
No single pruning recipe is universally safe: even within one architecture, the optimal method reverses across suites---L2 norm leads by $+$8\,pp on one task type yet trails by $-$5\,pp on another.
We propose \emph{Diagnose-then-Compress}: the coefficient of variation (CV) of post-connector token norms, computable in one forward pass, predicts both the compressibility class and the optimal scoring method without closed-loop evaluation.
For architectures where every deletion strategy fails, a lightweight re-encoding module (${\sim}$5\% extra parameters) recovers $>$60\% success rate at 75\% compression, establishing deletion itself---not token redundancy---as the failure mechanism.
\end{abstract}

tool_args.new_text:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models encode observations as hundreds of vision tokens, creating a computational bottleneck for real-time robotic control. Token pruning offers a training-free remedy, yet its effect varies dramatically across architectures: at retention ratio $k{=}0.95$, $\pi_{0.5}$ preserves 98\% task success while SmolVLA collapses to 0\%---why?

We identify the vision-language connector as the primary architectural factor governing pruning tolerance. The coefficient of variation (CV) of post-connector token norms, computable in a single forward pass, predicts compressibility across the full architecture spectrum: from CV$\,{=}\,$0.038 (near-immune linear projection) to CV$\,{=}\,$0.314 (catastrophic pixel-shuffle collapse). A controlled pair---$\pi_0$ and OpenVLA, both encoding 256 vision tokens through different connectors---yields CV values of 0.038 vs.\ 0.215, capturing their divergent pruning responses without closed-loop evaluation. Across five VLA architectures (450\,M--7\,B parameters) and four LIBERO manipulation suites, token-independent connectors degrade gracefully, while token-entangling connectors exhibit abrupt cliffs: SmolVLA collapses when just 6 of 128 tokens are removed.

Importance-based selection is not universally beneficial---it can be actively harmful. L2 norm selection preserves 98\% success on $\pi_{0.5}$ where random yields 9\% (89\,pp gap at $k{=}0.9$), yet on X-VLA at aggressive ratios, random outperforms L2 norm by $+$28\,pp---a strategy reversal driven by connector entanglement. Task complexity amplifies these connector-dependent patterns: multi-step tasks magnify entangling-connector losses by up to $20{\times}$, whereas independent connectors show ${\leq}$11\,pp degradation. For architectures where all deletion strategies fail, a lightweight re-encoding module (${\sim}$5\% extra parameters) recovers $>$60\% success at 75\% compression, confirming that token deletion---not redundancy---is the failure mechanism.
